title: Soccer Bosses Want FIFA to Share $2.1 Billion With 211 Countries
summary:
Soccer is the most popular sport on Earth. And the group that runs world soccer, FIFA, has a lot of money saved — about $6 billion. Now two leaders say it's time to share.

Aleksander Ceferin runs UEFA, the group in charge of soccer in Europe. Victor Montagliani runs CONCACAF, which covers North America, Central America and the Caribbean. Both are vice presidents of FIFA. On Friday, they sent a letter to FIFA President Gianni Infantino. In it, they asked for an independent review of FIFA's money and proposed giving $2.1 billion to FIFA's 211 member associations — the national soccer groups in each country.

That would mean at least $10 million for each member association during the 2027-30 cycle. The money would be on top of funding FIFA already gives through its Forward Programme. Countries could use it for fields, training and other soccer development.

Why is this happening? FIFA had a plan called FIFA Forward Enterprise. It would have sold a share of FIFA's competitions to outside investors to raise more money. But people didn't like that idea, and FIFA dropped it. Ceferin and Montagliani say their look at FIFA's numbers raises a question: was that plan even needed? They say FIFA can afford to give more from its own savings. Even after giving out $2.1 billion, they say, FIFA's reserves would stay above about $1.5 billion. They also want the other four continental confederations to support the idea. FIFA hasn't answered yet.
why_it_matters: Soccer is the game millions of kids play at recess, and this argument is really about who pays for the fields, coaches and balls that make those games possible.

background_read: FIFA (the group that runs world soccer) started in 1904 and is based in Zurich, Switzerland; it organizes the World Cup, a giant tournament played every four years.

UEFA (the group in charge of soccer in Europe) runs competitions like the Champions League, and CONCACAF (which covers North America, Central America and the Caribbean) runs its own tournaments — leaders of both sit as FIFA vice presidents.

FIFA has 211 member associations, which is more members than the United Nations (the group where almost all countries meet, with 193 members), and it usually gives some of its World Cup money back to them to build fields and train coaches.
Article_Structure: WHO: Aleksander Ceferin (head of UEFA, Europe's soccer group) and Victor Montagliani (head of CONCACAF, the North America, Central America and Caribbean group), both FIFA vice presidents, wrote to FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

WHAT: They asked for an independent review of FIFA's money and for $2.1 billion to be shared with FIFA's 211 member associations — at least $10 million each in the 2027-30 cycle, on top of the Forward Programme.
WHERE: FIFA works worldwide through 211 national associations; UEFA covers Europe and CONCACAF covers North America, Central America and the Caribbean.

WHY: FIFA's plan to sell a share of its competitions to outside investors was dropped, and the two leaders say FIFA's own savings are big enough — its reserves would still stay above about $1.5 billion even after sharing.

perspectives.description: They say FIFA's numbers show the money is already there, so FIFA should hand more of its savings to the national soccer groups that need it.
They would gain the most, because $10 million could pay for training, fields and youth programs they could never afford on their own.
FIFA hasn't answered yet, and it may argue that its Forward Programme already shares money and that big reserves are needed for the future.
